sections.heading: 3 TSHA
sections.text: In this section, we introduce TSHA, a comprehensive benchmark specifically designed to evaluate the ability of vision-language models (VLMs) to assess safety hazards. Sec. 3.1 details the data sources of the training and test sets, as well as the rigorous filtering and quality control procedures implemented to ensure dataset reliability. Sec. 3.2 presents detailed statistics of the dataset, providing insights into its coverage and representativeness. Sec. 3.3 elaborates on the pipeline for generating text descriptions for each sample, ensuring consistent and accurate annotation of safety hazards. Finally, Sec. 3.4 explicitly defines the task formulation of TSHA, clarifying the evaluation objectives for VLMs’ safety hazard assessment capability. Figure 1 : Overview of image, video and question samples of TSHA datasets. 3.1 Data Source TSHA Training Set. We curate images from four complementary sources: Existing Indoor Datasets, Internet images, AIGC-generated images, and newly captured images. The entire training set was developed with the participation of 20 volunteers and took two months to complete. For existing indoor datasets, we selected NYU v2 [ 33 ] and MIT Indoor Scenes [ 30 ] due to their rich indoor scene coverage, encompassing 67 indoor categories and over 10,000 real-world images (no simulator or virtual content). This real-world data enables VLMs to learn the distribution of authentic safety hazards. For Internet images, we carefully selected and downloaded 63 high-quality videos of everyday home life from platforms such as YouTube and Bilibili, covering diverse domestic scenarios. These videos were split into static frames at 3 FPS, with irrelevant opening/closing frames (prologues/epilogues) manually removed. For AIGC-generated images, we employed state-of-the-art closed-source text-to-video and text-to-image large models, including Jimeng [ 13 ] , Hunyuan [ 35 ] , PixVerse, and HailuoAI. Specifically, we first used text-generation LLMs (Doubao [ 14 ] , Tongyi Qianwen [ 4 ] , and Deepseek [ 32 ] ) to generate prompts describing safety-hazard-containing scenarios. These prompts then guided the aforementioned video/image generation models to produce corresponding content. Videos were again decomposed into static frames at 3 FPS. For newly captured images, 20 volunteers recorded videos of real-world home and work scenes (bedrooms, kitchens, living rooms, toilets, studies, and offices). These authentic everyday scenarios were also split into individual frames at 3 FPS. TSHA Test Set. To rigorously evaluate the safety hazard assessment capabilities learned from the TSHA training data, we constructed a comprehensive test suite designed specifically to assess models’ generalization to challenging, real-world scenarios. Unlike traditional benchmarks with limited hazard diversity, our test set introduces greater complexity by integrating three complementary components: video sequences, panoramic images, and a carefully selected subset of the training data. For the newly added video sequences, we leveraged Sora2’s [ 5 ] advanced video generation capabilities to create dynamic indoor scenes with time-evolving safety hazards—challenging models to interpret risks across sequential frames, as required in real-world applications. For the newly added panoramic images, we used the Tencent Hunyuan World model [ 16 ] to generate comprehensive panoramic scenes containing multiple concurrent hazards. This enables a holistic assessment of hazard detection capabilities, rather than limiting evaluation to local scene analysis. The data generation pipeline is illustrated in Fig. 2 . Figure 2 : Data Generation Pipeline. The collected images and videos from the data source undergo a four-stage annotation process: scene description, preliminary hazard identification, final hazard verification, and human verification. Filtering and Quality Control. To ensure the reliability and quality of the dataset, particularly the AIGC-based samples, two PhD students in computer science manually inspected each data entry individually. All training and test samples were verified to satisfy three essential criteria: physical plausibility, requiring that image or video content adheres to real-world physical laws; realism of danger, ensuring that the depicted hazards are consistent with real-life safety scenarios; and semantic consistency, meaning that images and videos accurately represent the intended safety risks. This manual filtering step effectively eliminated all AI-generated images that violate physical constraints or contain excessively exaggerated content. 3.2 Data Statistics Overall Data Scale and Distributions. As illustrated in Fig. 3(a) and Fig. 3(b) , the final training set comprises a total of 80,102 question-answer (QA) pairs, derived from four data sources: existing datasets (28,172 samples, 35.2%), newly captured images (8,724 samples, 10.9%), internet images (25,942 samples, 32.4%), and AIGC-generated images (17,264 samples, 21.6%). Each image is paired with two QA pairs, resulting in 40,051 training images—broken down into 14,086 (existing datasets), 4,362 (newly captured images), 12,971 (internet images), and 8,632 (AIGC images). The final test set contains 1,707 QA pairs, with contributions from six sources: existing datasets (392 samples, 23.0%), newly captured images (102 samples, 6.0%), internet images (296 samples, 17.3%), AIGC-generated images (210 samples, 12.3%), Sora2-generated videos (400 samples, 23.4%), and Tencent Hunyuan world model panoramic images (307 samples, 18.0%). Notably, existing datasets, newly captured images, internet images, and AIGC images each map to two QA pairs per image, while Sora2 videos and panoramic images correspond to one QA pair per video/image. This results in 196, 51, 148, 105, 400, and 307 images/videos for existing datasets, newly captured images, internet images, AIGC images, Sora2, and panoramic images, respectively. Safety Hazards Frequency. To illustrate the distribution of safety hazard categories, we present a bar chart in Fig. 3(c) , showing the most frequent hazards and their occurrence counts. Compared to prior work, the TSHA dataset covers a substantially broader and more diverse set of safety hazards, including blocked escape routes and electrical shock. The most prevalent categories are tripping hazards (3,633), cluttered floors (2,933), fire risk (1,737), and blocked escape routes (1,327). (a) Train data distribution. (b) Test data distribution. (c) Top 15 safety hazards. Figure 3 : Dataset statistics. Fig. 3(a) demonstrates the training data distribution, Fig. 3(b) shows the test data distribution and Fig. 3(c) indicates the Top-15 safety hazards of TSHA. 3.3 Multimodal Dialogue Generation. We employ the GPT-4o [ 18 ] model to generate contextual, multi-turn dialogues through a carefully designed chain-of-thought reasoning process. Our methodology progressively guides the model through four distinct stages: Scene Description, Preliminary Hazards Identification, and Final Hazards Identification, ensuring systematic and reliable hazard analysis. In the Scene Description phase, the model is instructed to generate an objective and comprehensive account of the visual environment. The prompt explicitly directs the model to “carefully observe this indoor environment image” and “objectively describe all visible objects, their positions, and spatial relationships,” while explicitly prohibiting any safety-related judgments. This step establishes a factual, assumption-free foundation for subsequent analysis. Building on this description, the Preliminary Hazards Identification stage performs an initial risk scan across multiple predefined safety dimensions—namely, electrical safety, fire hazards, trip or fall risks, clutter and obstruction hazards, and other conditions that could lead to personal injury or property damage. The model systematically enumerates potential hazards, each accompanied by a concise rationale linking the observation to its associated risk, thereby constructing a preliminary hazard profile. The Final Hazards Identification phase enforces rigorous, evidence-based validation of each candidate hazard. For every identified risk, the model must: (1) cite specific visual evidence from the image; (2) assign a confidence level (high/medium/low); (3) differentiate genuine hazards from benign everyday scenarios; and (4) apply domain-specific rules—particularly for clutter and obstruction—to ensure consistent interpretation. This stage further incorporates misidentification analysis and confidence calibration to suppress false positives while preserving sensitivity to true hazards. The fourth step consists of human verification. To ensure that GPT-4o can accurately identify and describe safety hazards within images, the preceding steps adopt a chain-of-thought-based self-correction mechanism, enabling GPT-4o to serve as an automatic quality assessor for self-inspection and revision. To further validate the quality of the resulting dataset, we conduct human verification performed by two PhD students in computer science. Specifically, we employ a random sampling strategy, where 10% of the total samples are randomly selected for manual inspection. The results demonstrate that the textual annotations in the sampled samples are highly consistent with the actual safety hazards depicted in the images, which effectively guarantees the reliability and high quality of the final dataset. This four-stage pipeline maintains strict contextual continuity: each reasoning step explicitly builds upon the prior output, forming a coherent and traceable analytical chain. All assessments remain grounded in observable visual content, avoiding speculative inference. Finally, every generated example undergoes manual verification to guarantee question–answer consistency and annotation fidelity. 3.4 Task Formulation. To systematically evaluate the capability of vision-language models in identifying safety hazards, we design two complementary inference tasks based on carefully curated image–question pairs. The first task, Choice Question, comprises two subtypes: binary true/false questions and four-option single-choice questions. In the true/false variant, each question presents a statement about the presence or absence of a hazard in the image, and the model must select “true” or “false” accordingly. The single-choice variant evaluates the model’s ability to recognize and categorize specific hazard types. Each question provides four mutually exclusive options covering distinct hazard categories or the option “no hazard”, and the model is required to select the label that best describes the risk depicted in the image. The second task, Open-ended Question Answering, requires the model to comprehensively identify and describe all potential safety hazards in an image or video without any predefined answer choices. Unlike the constrained formats above, this task demands spontaneous generation of natural language responses that are not only accurate but also concise, coherent, and semantically complete. Consequently, it constitutes a more challenging evaluation setting, jointly assessing hazard detection accuracy, descriptive fidelity, and reasoning clarity.

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: In Sec. 4.1 , we introduce the training settins and metrics of the experiments. In Sec. 4.2 , we evaluate the performance of previously representative VLM models on our TSHA test sets benchmarks and present our analysis of the results. In Sec. 4.3 , we assess the model’s ability on other benchmarks to demonstrate that TSHA doesn’t degrade the model’s general ability. In Sec. 4.4 , we conducted several ablation studies on the effects of training with different subsets of training sets and different evaluators. We report the results of the trained model on the other general benchmark. 4.1 Experimental Setup Training settings. To demonstrate the effectiveness of TSHA’s training sets, we utilize Qwen2.5-VL-3B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-32B, Ovis2-1B, and Minicpm-4B as baselines, training these models in GRPO algorithm [ 32 ] based on the ms-swift framework [ 45 ] and report the results and analysis. All expeiments are conducted on 8 NVIDIA H200-141G GPUs. In addition, we tested the TSHA-tuned Qwen2.5-VL model on other general benchmark sets. We evaluated five benchmark sets based on VLMEvalkit [ 10 ] : BLINK [ 11 ] , AI2D [ 20 ] , MMStar [ 6 ] , MUIRBench [ 37 ] , and SEEDBench2 [ 21 ] . Metrics. To evaluate model performance, we use accuracy as the metric for True/False and choice questions, as it effectively captures correctness in these constrained formats. For subjective question-answering (QA), however, evaluation is more challenging: traditional NLP metrics (e.g., BLEU-4, CIDEr) are insufficient due to their limited semantic understanding and inability to model long-range contextual dependencies. Recent work has demonstrated the promise of large language models (LLMs) as evaluators, leveraging their robust semantic comprehension. Building on this, we develop a specialized evaluation framework for indoor safety hazard QA pairs. Specifically, we employ ChatGPT-4o [ 18 ] to assess model responses against reference answers across three dimensions: (1) Accuracy (factual correctness and completeness of hazard identification), (2) Conciseness (efficiency and redundancy of the response), and (3) Coherence (structural organization and logical flow of the explanation). Each response is evaluated in multiple rounds, with scores averaged to ensure reliability. The final benchmark score is the mean of all sample-level scores, and the overall QA score is a weighted sum, yielding a comprehensive and statistically sound evaluation, which is shown as: S QA = 0.7 ⋅ S accuracy + 0.2 ⋅ S conciseness + 0.1 ⋅ S coherence , S_{\text{QA}}=0.7\cdot S_{\text{accuracy}}+0.2\cdot S_{\text{conciseness}}+0.1\cdot S_{\text{coherence}}, (1) where S accuracy S_{\text{accuracy}} , S conciseness S_{\text{conciseness}} , and S coherence S_{\text{coherence}} denote the respective scores for accuracy, conciseness, and coherence. We adopt such a weighting scheme based on the practical significance of each metric in safety hazard detection. Accuracy is assigned the highest weight since it directly determines the reliability of hazard identification, which is closely related to personal safety and property protection and thus represents the most critical factor. Conciseness is given the second-highest weight, as timely model responses are essential in safety - critical scenarios to enable rapid intervention and countermeasures. Coherence characterizes whether the model can provide logically consistent and complete descriptions of all identified safety hazards. For multiple-choice questions, we directly used answer accuracy as the score S CQ S_{\text{CQ}} . The final overall performance is reported as the average of the QA and choice-question scores: S overall = S QA + S CQ 2 , S_{\text{overall}}=\frac{S_{\text{QA}}+S_{\text{CQ}}}{2}, (2) where S QA S_{\text{QA}} represents the evaluated score for open-ended QA responses from the LLM, and S CQ S_{\text{CQ}} denotes the accuracy on multiple-choice questions. Our key findings are summarized as follows: Our benchmark presents a significant challenge to current vision-language models (VLMs). Notably, even state-of-the-art closed-source models achieved an average score of only 66.06: Claude-3.7-Sonnet attained the highest score (82.5), while Claude-4-Sonnet performed the worst (47.5). This indicates that newer models do not necessarily outperform older counterparts in safety hazard assessment, and VLMs’ ability to detect security vulnerabilities remains underdeveloped. Furthermore, open-source models exhibit more inconsistent performance. Despite an average score of 63.52, their performance fluctuates drastically: InternVL2.5-26B led with 82.8, whereas Gemma3-4B achieved only 34.5. We hypothesize that this discrepancy stems primarily from the scarcity of safety hazard assessment datasets and training resources, limiting model improvement and inducing substantial performance variability. Notably, Ovis2-1B, Minicpm-4B, and Qwen series models showed an average score improvement of 10.2 points after training on the TSHA dataset—with Qwen2.5-VL-3B achieving the largest gain (18.3 points). This validates the TSHA dataset’s effectiveness in enhancing VLMs’ security vulnerability detection capabilities. Motivated by this, we collected and released TSHA as a valuable resource for the open-source community, aiming to address the existing gap in VLMs’ performance for this critical task. In addition, to ensure the integrity of the experiment, we designed two test question types: open-ended QA questions and choice questions. Without pre-training, most models performed well on the choice questions, especially the InternVL series, achieving an accuracy of 80 % 80\% to 90 % 90\% . However, the open-ended QA questions were extremely challenging: all models struggled with them, achieving an accuracy of only around 60 % 60\% . Therefore, although we reported results for both question types to ensure the integrity of the study, we strongly recommend that researchers adopt the open-ended QA assessment method to obtain more realistic evaluation results, as choice questions cannot determine whether a model has the ability to identify safety hazards, and open-ended QA questions are more common and practical in reality. Notably, the most substantial gain is observed in the Qwen2.5-VL-3B model, where the overall performance is enhanced by 1.6 points compared to its baseline counterpart. This pronounced improvement highlights the effectiveness of TSHA in boosting the performance of lightweight vision-language models (VLMs), which are crucial for deployment in resource-constrained safety-critical scenarios. Importantly, even for the most powerful and state-of-the-art large-scale model in the Qwen2.5-VL series—Qwen2.5-VL-72B, which already exhibits strong baseline performance on general benchmarks—TSHA-based training still yields consistent and non-trivial improvements. This finding underscores the generalizability of the TSHA framework, as it is not limited to low-capacity models but also effectively augments the capabilities of high-performance large models. The results reveal a pronounced synergistic effect: while each data source individually improves upon the baseline, their integration yields further performance gains. Notably, the model trained on the full TSHA dataset—which unifies all four sources—achieves the highest overall performance. This demonstrates that the diverse data sources complement one another, collectively enriching the model’s perception and reasoning capabilities. Consequently, our findings underscore the necessity of the comprehensive data composition in TSHA for effective training in safety hazard assessment. To demonstrate the effectiveness of TSHA, we conduct an ablation study with different evaluators, as presented in Tab. 5 . Three LLMs—GPT-4o [ 18 ] , Claude-3.7-sonnet [ 3 ] , and Deepseek-r1 [ 32 ] —are employed as evaluators to assess the performance of vision-language models. To further validate TSHA in a comprehensive manner and alleviate potential biases from LLM-based evaluation, we additionally conduct a human evaluation. We recruit 50 participants, including computer science PhD and master’s students as well as practitioners from various industries. Each volunteer is randomly assigned 15 samples with corresponding model-generated risk descriptions and rates them along three dimensions: accuracy, conciseness, and coherence. Experimental results show that, under all three LLM evaluators, TSHA-trained models consistently outperform their baseline counterparts in safety hazard detection. This improvement is especially notable for the Qwen2.5-VL-3B model, whose overall scores are boosted by 10.4, 11.2, and 9.3 under GPT-4o, Claude-3.7-sonnet, and Deepseek-r1, respectively. In human evaluation, the overall scores of the Qwen2.5-VL 3B, 7B, and 32B variants are improved by 2.4, 2.1, and 0.6, respectively, confirming that TSHA-trained models generate more satisfactory responses from a human perspective.
